title: Quality-of-Transmission Estimation in Quantum Networks: Compute, Simulate, or Learn?
authors: Anis Bekri, Amar Abane, Van Sy Mai, Abdella Battou, Saddek Bensalem
abstract: Future quantum networks will rely on control-plane decisions such as routing, scheduling, entanglement provisioning, purification, and memory allocation. Each decision depends on a timely and reliable estimate of the quality of the entanglement that a candidate path can deliver, with end-to-end fidelity as a central metric. Inspired by the optical-networking experience with quality-of-transmission (QoT) estimation, this article asks when a quantum controller should compute fidelity analytically, simulate it, or learn a surrogate model. The optical analogy is useful but incomplete: optical QoT estimation often predicts a scalar transmission margin, whereas quantum QoT estimation must account for probabilistic entanglement generation, random memory waiting times, decoherence, state consumption, and measurement constraints that can make fidelity a stochastic target. We propose a compute/simulate/learn framework for quantum QoT estimation and illustrate it with a simulation-based proof of concept. Our study shows that analytical composition can be sufficient in simple regimes, that simulation becomes necessary when stochastic memory effects shape the delivered fidelity distribution, and that lightweight learned surrogates can approximate simulator labels at much lower runtime cost for online control. We close with open challenges for deployment, including stochastic targets, sim-to-real transfer, data-generation cost, physics-informed learning, and generalization beyond individual paths to full network topologies.
summary: This work tackles the critical problem of estimating entanglement quality in quantum networks by comparing analytical, simulation, and machine learning approaches. The authors demonstrate that while simple formulas fail under decoherence, a trained ML surrogate can provide highly accurate, real-time fidelity estimates. This framework is vital for enabling robust, scalable quantum network control planes.
main_problem: The paper addresses how to optimally estimate the Quality-of-Transmission (QoT) or end-to-end fidelity in quantum networks for real-time control decisions.
main_result: A learned surrogate model can achieve simulator-grade accuracy at formula-grade speed, effectively bridging the gap between computationally expensive simulation and inaccurate analytical approximations.
method: The authors propose and evaluate a compute/simulate/learn framework, training machine learning surrogates on data generated by a full quantum network simulator.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a quantum network relying on distributed entanglement, involving elementary links, entanglement swapping, and quantum memories subject to decoherence.
key_observables: End-to-end fidelity of the delivered entangled state, which can be a point estimate or a full probability distribution.
important_parameters: Decoherence rates, waiting times, link fidelities, and the computational cost/runtime constraints for online decision-making.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the fidelity estimation task can be decomposed into regimes where analytical, simulated, or learned methods are optimal; the analogy to optical QoT is noted as incomplete.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the decision workflow comparing analytical, simulation, and ML approaches; one shows the learning curve where the surrogate overtakes the analytical formula, and another demonstrates generalization across different path link-length regimes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by contrasting the limitations of analytical formulas (failing with decoherence) and full simulation (too slow). It then introduces and validates the ML surrogate approach, showing its superior performance in speed and accuracy over both alternatives for online control.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, practical methodology for handling complex, time-dependent quantum channel characterization, which is crucial for scaling quantum communication networks beyond idealized models.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Entanglement distribution along a repeater path. Elementary links are generated probabilistically and then fused by Bell-state measurements at intermediate repeaters. The final end-to-end fidelity is affected not only by the elementary-link qualities, but also by swap imperfections and memory decoherence accumulated while neighboring links wait.

Fig. 2. Decision-aware machine-learning workflow for quantum QoT estimation. The upper part shows the offline training workflow: candidate path configurations are evaluated with a quantum-network simulator to produce fidelity labels, build a QoT dataset, and train a machine- learning surrogate. The lower part shows the online decision flow: a fidelity-estimation request is mapped to analytical computation when the formula is valid and its inputs are fresh, detailed simulation when runtime allows, or the trained machine-learning surrogate when repeated simulation is too costly at decision time.

Fig. 3. Learning the expected fidelity. a) Five-fold cross-validated error of six regressors against the per-fold-calibrated formula; tree ensembles cut the error ∼5–6×. b) Learning curve: the surrogate overtakes the formula after ∼80 configurations and keeps improving.

Fig. 4. Generalization to unseen path regimes. Leave-one-family- out error over 270 paths (90 per family; train on two of ring/grid/backbone, test on the third) beside pooled-interpolation error; every model beats the formula on each unseen family, and extrapolation is close to interpolation.
